editorial.headline: Government Clinics, With No PMA Route in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 86104 covers comprehensive government clinic care, from primary to further services and outpatient to inpatient settings, and is closed to foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register KBLI 86104 in Bali today. The activity is the classification for government clinic activity: comprehensive health-care and physical-treatment services that provide primary care and/or further health services. Its defining feature is the public organiser. Services may be run by the central government—through ministries or institutions, the police, or the armed forces—or by regional government. The scope also distinguishes clinics by service capability, identifying Klinik Pratama and Klinik Utama, with either outpatient or inpatient arrangements. It includes special government health clinics for athletes.

Every government Klinik Pratama and Klinik Utama is expressly included. The record makes the activity available across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Those scale labels tell us the breadth of the classification, while the named public bodies tell us who may organise the service. The classification goes beyond one level of clinic and beyond one mode of attendance. By naming both Pratama and Utama clinics and both outpatient and inpatient formats, the scope preserves the distinctions that frame the services, without departing from government organisation. It is a precise description of the government-clinic field set out in the record, rather than a general label for health care.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership position is decisive. The PMA status is TERTUTUP and maximum foreign ownership is 0%. There is no foreign equity available under this record, and no PMA registration route for the activity in Indonesia. The national source cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The fact that the activity is listed across four scales does not change that result: scale coverage identifies the listed scales, whereas the PMA field states the foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali carries the same PMA conclusion: TERTUTUP, with the activity marked blocked. But the record makes an important distinction about the provincial moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; it is therefore not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk PMA activities. That absence of a moratorium block is not an opening. Bali’s status remains closed, exactly as the national 0% ceiling leaves no foreign ownership. The honest reading is uncomplicated: this government-clinic activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: That absence of a moratorium block is not an opening.
